title: Laser Weapons Are Finally Going to Battle: The US Military Has Already Spent $15 Billion on R&D
dek: Lasers are called the sniper rifles of directed energy weapons, while microwaves are the electronic shotgun. The US military is shifting from R&D to procurement, but the real shortage is cheap interceptors—can you win every engagement but still lose the war because you can't afford it? That's the key.
why: This episode explains the real bottlenecks of laser weapons from physics principles and operational economics, and also touches on supply chains and the defense procurement landscape. It's suitable for those interested in defense tech and defense stocks.
who: Defense industry analysts, defense tech VCs, readers following China's military modernization, and anyone wanting to understand the US military's ammunition consumption anxiety.
skip: The first few minutes of event promos and small talk can be skipped to 05:08 where the guest's military background begins.

points.h: Lasers are sniper rifles, microwaves are shotguns
points.body: Wayne uses the analogy "lasers are sniper rifles, microwaves are electronic shotguns" to distinguish the two types of directed energy weapons: lasers concentrate energy into a narrow beam, attacking one target at a time, burning through with thermal energy; microwaves have a wider beam and can affect the electronics of multiple targets simultaneously. The Government Accountability Office notes that high-power microwaves can reach peak power of 100 megawatts, but comparing that directly to the kilowatts of continuous-wave lasers is meaningless because the two are fundamentally different: lasers try to increase power, microwaves try to amplify area effects. The choice depends on the target—drone swarms suit microwaves, while a single ballistic missile can only be engaged with a laser. This is because microwaves can disable drones and make them fall, but unlike lasers, they cannot destroy a single high-speed missile.

points.h: Chemical lasers failed due to size and logistics
points.body: After the laser was invented in the 1960s, the military immediately saw its potential, but the real problems were power and size. In the 1990s, the US-Israeli "Tactical High Energy Laser" and DARPA's MIRACLE chemical laser both successfully shot down rockets, but the systems were huge and logistically complex, leading to program termination in 2006. Chemical lasers get light energy directly from chemical reactions and don't need electricity—for example, the oxygen-iodine laser was mounted on a Boeing 747 (YAL-1) to try to intercept ballistic missiles near their launch areas, but carrying chemicals on an aircraft was too dangerous. Today's key metric for technological progress is called SWaP: size, weight, and power. In the past, lasers were as large as a building because they required enormous amounts of electricity to generate the beam; today's goal is to fit them into trucks and warships.

points.h: The bottleneck for handheld lasers is power compression
points.body: When asked why sci-fi handheld laser guns don't exist yet, Wayne points out that the bottleneck is "power generation and compression." Currently, the fastest land platform is a high-energy laser mounted on a Stryker armored vehicle, with a power of 50 kilowatts, relying on the vehicle's own power generation; if you need a 5-kilowatt beam to shoot down a drone, you might need 15 to 25 kilowatts of input power. Without sufficient power, you can only watch drones fly toward you with no way to respond. Electricity is the core constraint, not a gap in optical technology. This also explains why laser weapons have been in development for decades and are only now approaching the tipping point for large-scale deployment.

Many people think lasers can replace multi-million-dollar interceptor missiles, but Wayne warns that if the enemy launches hypersonic weapons, you wouldn't want to gamble on a laser hitting a Mach 5 target precisely. Therefore, the real framework is "integrated air and missile defense"—a combination of layered defenses. Lasers and microwaves have the cost advantage of low per-shot cost, but they require the target to come within a kill range; against weapons traveling at 4,000 miles per hour, you still need carefully designed interceptors like PAC-3 and SM-3. Israel is the best example: Arrow 2/3 intercepts long-range ballistic missiles, David's Sling handles medium-range threats, Iron Dome stops rockets, and now Iron Beam is added for drones.

points.h: Battlefield commanders don't care about unit cost
points.body: When asked who thinks about cost when opening fire, Wayne divides decision-making into four levels: tactical, operational, strategic, and national. Frontline platoon and company commanders, when facing threats, will use any means necessary to protect their troops and don't care about missile costs; but at the theater commander and Pentagon level, they must consider whether it's worth using a $4.1 million PAC-3 to shoot down a $30,000 drone. So the demand for "cheap weapons" comes from the top, not the grassroots. Only national-level decision-makers incorporate ammunition consumption and supply chain issues into their choices. This distinction explains why the US military, after being attrited in Yemen and the Red Sea, has begun shifting toward low-cost interception solutions.

points.h: The US military is shifting to low-cost munitions
points.body: Over the past few decades, the US military has stockpiled increasingly expensive precision interceptors for high-end peer warfare, but in Yemen and the Red Sea, it was forced to change because drones were attriting its supplies. Wayne says the Pentagon is signing multi-year framework agreements to significantly increase production, but the core realization is that you can't always use expensive solutions against cheap threats. His key judgment: in future conflicts, "you can win every engagement but still lose the war economically." This is the market demand for low-cost interceptors like Coyote, Vampire, and APKWS. Battlefield commanders need more options at hand, not just the ability to fire expensive missiles until they run out.

points.h: Startups are entering the mid-tier market
points.body: When asked whether laser weapons might be stifled by defense giants due to the innovator's dilemma, Wayne believes that giants will indeed continue to dominate the high-end interceptor market, but the low-end and mid-tier solutions have already been awarded to five companies with Department of Defense contracts: Coaspire, Leidos, Anduril, Zone 5, and Castilian. The DoD wants tens of thousands of units, not an increase from 620 to 2,000. So in the short term, giants dominate, but within three to five years, newcomers like Anduril may capture the mid-tier market. This also means that when investing in defense stocks, you can't just look at traditional giants; you need to see who benefits from the procurement shift.

points.h: AI killer robots are still far away
points.body: Wayne says that in the Pentagon, AI is currently used only for intelligence analysis, image labeling for analysts, and change detection, not for strike decisions. His previous research at the war college was centered on "AI and levels of trust." Between target identification and tactical strike, it remains fully "human-in-the-loop"—AI can help you find targets and issue alerts, but the final decision is still made by human commanders and intelligence analysts. Some worry that AI might decide on its own to destroy targets, but Wayne says that future is still a long way off. The risk models aren't ready, so the Pentagon currently does not use AI for autonomous killing; instead, it uses AI for military intelligence screening to replace tedious work.
